cues.text: Section four is about dashboards and continuous improvement.
Let us begin with what a dashboard is.
A dashboard presents selected measurements and trends to support decisions.
Notice that it is selective: it does not show everything, only the measurements that help someone decide what to do.
Dashboards come in three kinds, according to their purpose.
Operational dashboards focus on immediate health, meaning how the system is doing right now.
Tactical dashboards track team performance and improvement over time.
Strategic dashboards summarise business value and risk, and so serve those who look at the organisation as a whole.
Next, what makes a dashboard useful.
A useful dashboard identifies seven things: the metric, the baseline, the target, the current value, the trend, the owner and the reporting interval.
The metric tells you what is being measured.
The baseline gives you the starting point for comparison, and the target tells you where you want to be.
The current value shows where you are now, while the trend shows the direction of movement.
The owner is the person or team responsible, and the reporting interval says how often the figure is reported.
There is also a guideline about alerts.
Use alerts for actionable deviations, rather than overwhelming teams with every minor fluctuation.
If people receive an alert for every small change, they stop paying attention, and the alerts that matter get lost.
Now let us look at the tools.
Monitoring tools such as Prometheus collect metrics.
Grafana visualises measurements.
ELK and Splunk support log analysis.
Distributed traces help identify slow dependencies, that is, which connected service is causing delay.
Business intelligence tools can combine operational and financial data, which lets you relate technical performance to business outcomes.
The second half of this section turns to improvement.
Use the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle.
First, plan an improvement.
Second, implement it.
Third, evaluate the results.
Fourth, standardise the approach if it worked, or revise it if it did not.
Then the cycle repeats.
Alongside it, root-cause analysis investigates why a problem occurred, rather than only treating its symptoms.
Two techniques help explore causes: the five whys and cause-and-effect diagrams.
However, evidence is necessary to validate conclusions.
A plausible explanation is not enough; you must confirm it with data.
Finally, consider an example.
A retailer sees slow page loads during a campaign.
What should the team do?
Investigate request volume, database query latency, cache hit rates, external dependencies and resource saturation.
Importantly, do not immediately buy larger servers.
The bottleneck may be an inefficient query, and more hardware would not fix that.
After making an improvement, measure again, so that you can confirm the change actually worked.
That completes this section.
